Staging environment for tomorrow’s demo

standup.text:
Payments retries and rollout blockers

We reviewed the payments webhook fix, orders migration, search ranker results, and auth rollout blocker. The webhook fix is merged, while auth production rollout remains blocked on staging verification; the Kubernetes upgrade date still needs confirmation.

## Action items
- [ ] Finish the webhook retry dashboard panel by end of tomorrow (me)
- [ ] Check whether last week’s SDK upgrade caused Jen’s feature flag evaluation latency bump (me)
- [ ] Send Priya the billing service audience configuration notes today (me)
- [ ] Confirm the Kubernetes upgrade date in the channel (me)
- [ ] Finish the orders migration rollback path by Thursday (Tomasz)
- [ ] Gather at least another week of search traffic before reporting results to product (Jen)
- [ ] Paste the platform ticket for the staging identity provider issue in the channel (Priya)

## Payments webhook retries
- The merged fix stops payments callbacks from retrying indefinitely on 4xx responses; retries now back off and stop after five attempts.
- The dashboard panel was estimated at half a day to a day of work.

## Orders migration
- Tomasz ran the orders table migration script against a full staging copy in about 40 minutes, with no locks observed.
- The rollback path is half-written; certificate renewal work interrupted it.

## Search relevance and flag latency
- Jen’s new ranker entered shadow mode on Monday. Click-through is up about 0.4%, but that is within noise and not yet evidence of a win.
- Shadow traffic goes through the feature flag service, where Jen observed a roughly 8 ms p99 evaluation latency increase.
- I suspect the SDK version I upgraded last week may be responsible.

## Auth rollout blocker
- Priya’s session-token refactor is basically done, with everything moved off the old cookie helper.
- The staging identity provider cannot issue tokens with the new audience claim. Staging verification is required for production sign-off, so this effectively blocks production rollout.
- The platform team has agreed to investigate but is swamped; timing could be today or next week.
- A similar billing service issue required adding the audience to the identity provider’s allowed list; this may also be a configuration issue.

## Kubernetes upgrade
- I think the upgrade moved to the 20th because of the freeze, but the date is unconfirmed.

## Open questions
- When will the platform team resolve the staging identity provider blocker?

hiring.text:
Rahul Venkataraman hiring debrief

We reviewed Rahul Venkataraman’s four interview rounds for the senior backend role. Strong system design and positive hiring-manager feedback were balanced by mixed coding results; we agreed to move forward to reference checks, with particular attention to team dynamics and attrition.

## Decisions
- Move Rahul forward to reference checks.

## Action items
- [ ] Contact the recruiter today to request two former-manager references and one peer reference (me).
- [ ] Ask references about Rahul’s possible role in team attrition, how he worked with the team, whether teammates would work with him again, and how he handles losing a technical argument (me).
- [ ] Send the debrief summary after the meeting (me).

## System design
- Priya gave a strong hire signal: Rahul asked about write volume upfront, independently proposed event-store partitioning, and handled rebalance questions well, including backpressure and idempotent consumers.
- Rahul acknowledged that he had not run the broker in production and would check its failover semantics before committing to it; Priya viewed that honesty positively.

## Coding
- Dmitri leaned no hire, but not a hard no: Rahul completed interval merging after roughly ten minutes on an incorrect approach, then did not finish concurrent cache eviction.
- In Dmitri’s second problem, the structure and locking were mostly right, but Rahul ran out of time and struggled to explain a race condition.
- Imani leaned hire: Rahul finished both problems with clean code and proactively wrote tests.
- Imani wanted more evidence of how Rahul scopes work: he asked few clarifying questions on the second problem, though he handled the edge case she had planned to raise.

## Motivation and team dynamics
- Lena’s hiring-manager feedback was positive overall. Rahul wants to leave because he has spent two years maintaining a monolith and wants to build new things, rather than for money.
- Rahul described losing a rewrite disagreement with his previous manager and accepting the outcome, while acknowledging that he would have pushed harder on one part.
- Lena did not have time to explore a passing comment that seemed to imply Rahul may have contributed to team attrition. It was unclear whether this reflected humility or a genuine concern.
- Priya had not explored team dynamics in her technical round and considered the attrition concern worth asking about, but not a dealbreaker.

## Open questions
- How should the conflicting coding signals be weighed, particularly around concurrency and problem scoping?

oneonone.text:
Ingestion redesign and career growth

Daniela and I discussed moving toward design ownership and cross-team technical leadership, with the ingestion redesign as a possible opportunity. We agreed to start with a short proposal, sharpen the billing postmortem, and update the rollback runbook; the staff track remains a possibility, not a promise.

## Decisions
- Start the ingestion redesign with a one-page proposal rather than a full design doc, initially for Daniela and written so Marcus can read it without prior context.
- Prioritize the proposal over the rollback runbook, which is not urgent.
- Meet again at the same time next week.

## Action items
- [ ] Draft the ingestion redesign proposal with the problem, a couple of options, and a rough estimate; flag unknowns and send it to Daniela this Friday, or notify her if it slips to Monday (me).
- [ ] Give the alerting gap its own section in the postmortem and sharpen the contributing factors (me).
- [ ] Add the outdated rollback runbook to the postmortem as an action item owned by me, and update the runbook; tentatively aim for the end of next week, with timing flexible (me).
- [ ] Ping Joaquin for ingestion cluster metrics and ask for twenty minutes, with Daniela's backing (me).
- [ ] Look into the ingestion redesign's potential overlap with Priya's team and loop me into the downstream-consumer context (Daniela).
- [ ] Decide who else should see the proposal after reviewing it (Daniela).

## Design ownership and staff track
- I've spent about eight months on integrations, bug fixes, and migrations and want to design work, not only implement others' designs.
- I'm interested in both architecture and project technical leadership, including owning a design doc end to end; Q3 felt doable as a possible target.
- Daniela praised the retry-logic design doc from last spring and noted that Marcus had highlighted it in review.
- Daniela said the staff-track path depends substantially on successful ingestion work and demonstrating cross-team scope. A strong proposal followed by leading the work would be a meaningful signal, but the opportunity is not a test or a promotion promise.

## Ingestion redesign scope
- The redesign has been in the backlog for a long time and is considered difficult.
- One version may conflict with Priya's team's downstream-consumer work; Daniela wants to avoid a cross-team ownership conflict without context.
- Current throughput numbers are uncertain. Rough estimates are acceptable if unknowns are explicit; Joaquin has the ingestion cluster dashboards and probably set up most of them.

## Billing rollout and postmortem
- The billing service rolled out Tuesday, mostly smoothly. A smaller recurrence of the cache issue was caught in staging, reflecting the value of the postmortem work.
- Daniela thought the root-cause section was good, but the contributing factors needed more detail.
- Alerting did not fire for forty minutes. I was concerned about making Dev's on-call setup look bad; Daniela emphasized recording actionable facts to prevent another incident rather than assigning blame.

## Open questions
- Will I own and lead the ingestion redesign, and what scope would avoid overlap with Priya's team?
- How might successful cross-team ingestion work translate into progress toward the staff track?

sales.text:
Lintly pilot for Harbor Freight Logistics

We explored Lintly for Harbor Freight Logistics’ PR review delays and outlined a six-week platform-team pilot. The kickoff is tentatively the seventh, pending platform-team confirmation; security approval remains a blocker because procurement requires SOC 2 Type II and Lintly currently has Type I.

## Decisions
- Plan a six-week pilot with approximately 8–10 platform-team developers, with success criteria defined together.
- Keep the pilot warn-only for at least the first two weeks; security-only blocking may be enabled afterward.
- Treat the first week as setup and exclude it from adoption metrics.
- Include the optional pre-commit hook in the pilot scope.

## Action items
- [ ] Send the SOC 2 Type I report and penetration-test summary today (me).
- [ ] Check with compliance about obtaining an auditor bridge letter and follow up by Thursday (me).
- [ ] Confirm whether Enterprise on-prem scoping is worth pursuing alongside the security review (me).
- [ ] Put a tentative hold on the seventh for pilot kickoff (me).
- [ ] Add the pre-commit hook to the pilot setup document (me).
- [ ] Send a quote for 39 active seats on Business (me).
- [ ] Seek manager approval for a pilot rate and return with a number before Thursday (me).
- [ ] Send the follow-up email within the next hour (me).
- [ ] Confirm the seventh and the pilot group with the platform lead (Marcus).
- [ ] Take the security questions to legal and check whether a bridge letter is acceptable under the Type II policy (Marcus).

## Review workflow and Lintly fit
- The team has approximately 45 engineers, including six contractors; two contractors leave at month-end.
- Median time to first review is about three days, followed by another one or two days of back-and-forth. Senior reviewers spend time on style, naming, unused imports and unhandled error returns rather than logic.
- Previous linters produced roughly 900 warnings on day one and were disabled because of noise.
- CI is mostly Jenkins, with frequent pipeline timeouts; the mobile driver app team uses some GitHub Actions. Lintly supports both without requiring consolidation.
- Lintly surfaces enforced rules by severity and suppresses existing findings through a baseline scan, so PRs show only newly introduced issues.

## Pricing and pilot measurement
- Team costs $22 per active developer per month, billed annually, with core rules, Jenkins and GitHub Actions integrations, and standard support.
- Business costs $38 per active developer per month and adds custom rules, SSO and audit logs. Enterprise has custom pricing, on-prem deployment and a dedicated success manager.
- Active seats count developers who opened or commented on a PR in the previous 30 days. I estimated approximately 39 active seats, depending on churn.
- Business supports SAML and SCIM with Okta for automatic provisioning and deprovisioning; audit logs can be exported to a SIEM. Okta SSO is non-negotiable for Harbor Freight Logistics.
- Proposed pilot measures include review cycle time, style-related review comments and developer sentiment, with a baseline from Jenkins and GitHub data during the first week. Review cycle time is the VP’s priority.
- Marcus requested a paid pilot rate, suggesting half price for the first six weeks to simplify approval; no rate was approved.
- A release freeze in the first week of the month likely covers only production deployments, but could slow adoption because engineers will be busy.

## Security and deployment
- Lintly analyzes source code in memory and retains findings metadata, not source code. Customer code is not used for model training, as stated in the terms and DPA.
- Lintly received SOC 2 Type I in March. The Type II observation window runs through the end of Q3, with the report expected in October.
- Harbor Freight Logistics’ procurement policy requires Type II for vendors with source-code access. A current report plus a bridge letter was raised as a possible approval path, subject to legal review.
- On-prem deployment is Enterprise-only and usually requires a few weeks of setup with the solutions team. Keeping code inside Harbor Freight Logistics’ VPC could potentially address the security concern.
- Secret scanning detects common credential patterns and high-entropy strings. It can block PR merges; local commit blocking requires the pre-commit hook. It complements rather than replaces a secrets vault or GitHub push protection.

## Open questions
- Will legal approve SaaS access before the Type II report is available, or will an Enterprise on-prem deployment be needed?
- Which exact success thresholds and security rules should the pilot use?
- Will security-only blocking be enabled after the first two weeks?

planning.text:
Q1 feature scope and priorities

We narrowed Q1 to five committed features, with a scoped-down offline sync as the headline, pending leadership confirmation. Notion and Evernote import remain deferred to Q2, enterprise SSO moves to Q2 scoping, and AI summaries remain an experiment rather than a committed feature.

## Decisions
- Commit five Q1 features: template gallery, styled PDF export, offline sync, a minimal sharing-permissions fix, and an iOS quick-capture widget.
- Target template gallery internal dogfooding this week and external beta at the end of January, with January 20 as the lazy-loading checkpoint.
- Scope offline sync to last-writer-wins with visible conflict copies, subject to leadership confirmation; revisit proper merging in Q2 if the data supports it.
- Limit permissions work to a clear effective-permission display explaining folder versus direct access. Defer enterprise SSO and group mapping to Q2 scoping, with no delivery date committed.
- Launch the quick-capture widget on iOS first, not Android in Q1.
- Keep Notion and Evernote import in Q2 because of parser complexity and formatting-loss risks, particularly Evernote nested tables.
- Run an AI-summary waitlist test, but do not list AI summaries as a committed Q1 feature.

## Action items
- [ ] Record the import deferral and nested-table rationale in the roadmap document (me).
- [ ] Confirm the scoped offline-sync plan with leadership (me).
- [ ] Bring AI-summary cost numbers to the next sync (me).
- [ ] Add an explicit requirement to the offline-sync spec that release notes explain possible duplicate notes (me).
- [ ] Block an hour Thursday afternoon to review the template gallery empty state (me).
- [ ] Prepare the template gallery empty-state design by Thursday and show it Thursday afternoon (Sven).
- [ ] Design the effective-permission panel within a week (Sven).
- [ ] Keep the offline-sync spec moving this week so Aiko can start scoping conflict-copy logic (owner unclear).

## Template gallery and PDF export
- Gallery backend is merged behind a flag; thumbnail lazy loading remains, estimated at half a day.
- Gallery design reuses the search card component.
- PDF export can reuse the HTML styling engine through a renderer; estimate is one to two engineering weeks, with fonts a possible complication.

## Offline sync
- Support demand centers on editing offline and syncing after reconnecting. Cached reading already exists partially, but older notes are not guaranteed to be available.
- Roughly 40% of last quarter’s sync-related tickets concerned lost edits or stale note versions.
- Full CRDT text merging was estimated at six to eight engineer-weeks for the core, plus three to four weeks for mobile clients—roughly a quarter for two engineers.
- The scoped version is estimated at three to four engineering weeks and roughly two design weeks. Conflict copies can create confusing duplicates when devices edit different parts of the same note.
- Sven explored a quiet cloud icon, an offline banner, and per-note indicators. The UI needs to distinguish locally saved edits, pending sync, and conflicts without alarming users.
- A full conflict-resolution screen would take about two design weeks plus a week of usability testing.

## Permissions and mobile widget
- Aiko flagged scope creep around permissions: the current owner/editor/viewer model becomes confusing when folder and direct sharing overlap.
- The minimal fix is estimated at two engineering weeks and one design week; the panel should explain who has access and why.
- iOS quick capture is estimated at two weeks. Android requires separate work, and its widget API was described as fragile.
- Sven felt an iOS-first launch would be acceptable if communicated clearly, given the target segment’s iOS usage.

## AI-summary evidence and costs
- I favored a pilot because of competitive pressure and an existing model partnership; a basic API-backed summary card might take three weeks.
- Aiko questioned demand for summaries of users’ own notes, ongoing inference costs, and quality on messy notes, and wanted at least a month of cost modeling plus a small user test before committing engineering time.
- Sven favored a fake summary button leading to a waitlist to test demand before investing in design.
- The five committed features already represent roughly ten or eleven engineering weeks across people, raising concern that adding summaries could displace other work.

## Open questions
- Should an AI-summary pilot receive Q1 engineering time? I favor it; Aiko remains opposed without demand and cost evidence. Revisit at the next sync with cost numbers and waitlist-test evidence.

brainstorm.text:
Climbing booking app naming brainstorm

We brainstormed names and positioning for the climbing booking app without choosing a name. Topout, Slab and Rackly emerged as the main candidates, with trademark checks and more tagline exploration ahead of Thursday.

## Action items
- [ ] Pull trademark searches for Topout and Slab tonight and send them around (me)
- [ ] Keep Belay on the list as a possible brand or feature name rather than a product name (me)
- [ ] Try taglines that do not lead with failure (owner unclear)
- [ ] Ask their mom about Beta again (owner unclear)

## Positioning and audiences
- The booking problem is unclear availability around route-setting schedules and wall openings: climbers show up and get turned away.
- We leaned toward access as the core promise: “you’ll actually get on the wall,” with booking as the mechanism.
- Gym owners pay and sign contracts; climbers use the app and help it spread. The name needs to appeal to both.
- A neutral name with a climbing-specific tagline could balance those audiences, though immediate recognition may matter in a small niche.
- “Never get turned away at the door” felt strong but led with failure; “book your wall” drew criticism for sounding like a hotel ad.

## Name candidates
- Topout implies finishing a climb and carries the access promise, but there may already be a gym-management company using it. It also drew a sports-drink comparison.
- Slab is short and climbing-related, but could sound like a flooring company or bakery.
- Rackly felt friendly to me; Tomás also liked it despite the boat-rental association.
- Beta and Cragline are parked. Beta has climbing and startup meanings, but could be mistaken for test software; Cragline evokes a route map but sounded like an airline.
- Belay conveys trust, but pronunciation concerns made it unlikely as the product name. “Belay alerts” and “belay queue” were floated as feature names.
- Dani’s initial ideas included Route, Crimp, Beta and a chalk-related name. Other suggestions included Gripfeed and Lead.
- Crux, Send, Basecamp and Clip were seen as crowded or already taken; Kit and Gear felt too vague or generic. Holdless, Wallmate, Climbin and Onwall were dismissed during brainstorming.

## Open questions
- Which of Topout, Slab and Rackly best fits the product?
- Should the main name signal climbing directly, or leave that work to the tagline and feature names?
- How should the brand balance gym-owner credibility with climber appeal?
- What positive tagline best expresses getting onto the wall?

design_review.text:
Payouts queue migration to Postgres

We agreed on a design direction for moving settlement jobs from Redis to Postgres while keeping webhook fanout on Redis for now. A prototype can proceed once the processor idempotency window and Go driver behavior are confirmed; production approval also requires load-test results.

## Decisions
- Move settlement jobs to Postgres using SKIP LOCKED and polling with backoff.
- Keep webhook fanout on Redis short term and revisit it after the Kafka consumer group work settles.
- Use a local idempotency table keyed by job ID, storing the processor response, rather than relying solely on the processor’s idempotency window.
- Gate the prototype on answers about the processor’s idempotency window and Go driver compatibility; require load-test numbers before greenlighting production.

## Action items
- [ ] Pull client error logs for both Redis incident windows and post findings in the design doc by the 23rd, stated as Thursday (me)
- [ ] Load-test the idempotency table by March 28 (me)
- [ ] Update the design doc with the review outcomes and tag owners (me)
- [ ] Write the fanout decision doc by the end of next sprint, March 14 (Greg)
- [ ] Review the pgbouncer pool configuration for worker compatibility, including session-level advisory locks and prepared statements (Ola)
- [ ] Confirm whether the Go driver uses prepared statements under the pool configuration by the 18th (Ola)
- [ ] Ask the processor account team to confirm the idempotency window (owner unclear)

## Migration rationale and scope
- Two incidents last quarter silently dropped jobs during Redis memory pressure. Postmortem INFO statistics showed rising evicted_keys, but client-side error handling still needs verification.
- Redis enqueue happens after the Postgres commit; a process crash between them can leave a ghost payout state.
- Postgres and pgbouncer are already operated, avoiding a new stateful system.
- Card processor retries account for ninety-something percent of queue volume; internal webhook fanout is small but latency-sensitive.
- Keeping both systems increases operational complexity. Kafka was raised as a possible later fanout destination, but additional topics are undesirable while consumer lag alerts remain noisy.

## Idempotency and throughput
- The proposed worker flow claims a row, marks it in_progress and commits, calls the processor outside the transaction using the job ID as the idempotency key, then marks completion in a second transaction.
- The sales deck suggests a 24-hour processor idempotency window, but retries can extend to about three days. A retry outside the window could double-charge.
- Storing the processor response locally would allow replaying the outcome without another processor call.
- Measured peak volume is about 340 payouts per second. One insert and one update per job would add roughly 700 writes per second on top of queue traffic; primary capacity is not yet load-tested.

## Latency and connection pooling
- Current Redis end-to-end p99 is around 40 ms, with sub-millisecond enqueue and near-instant dequeue when work is available.
- Proposed polling starts at 50 ms and backs off to 500 ms when empty. Under load, workers should find rows immediately; estimated p99 is perhaps 120 ms, with low confidence.
- LISTEN/NOTIFY is problematic through pgbouncer transaction pooling because a LISTEN connection cannot be held.
- Short claim transactions should fit transaction pooling, but long-running holds and session-level features could cause problems. Whether the Go driver’s simple protocol is enabled remains uncertain.

## Rollback and reconciliation
- The proposed rollback plan uses one week of dual-write to both queues, consuming from only one; rollback would flip the consumer.
- Fatima raised concerns about draining in-flight Postgres jobs and divergent writes causing duplicate or missing execution.
- A nightly job-ID reconciler exists under Priya’s team, but it is built for the ledger, not the queue.

## Open questions
- What is the processor’s confirmed idempotency window?
- Does the Go driver use cached prepared statements under the proposed pool configuration?
- How will queue-specific dual-write reconciliation and in-flight rollback handling work?

customer_support.text:
Northeast field team sync failures

We reproduced an offline sync failure on app version 4.11.3 running iOS eighteen point two: the device reported “synced,” but the test job was missing from the web dashboard. A workaround succeeded once, but no root cause, fix date, or invoice credit was confirmed.

## Action items
- [ ] Escalate the sync failure to the sync team today with reproduction steps, the affected northeast region, and the version rollout timeline (me)
- [ ] Send Marcus a written workaround for the field team (me)
- [ ] Send billing an escalation today with the estimated re-dispatch costs, the 41-of-163 report, reproduction steps, and version numbers; ask billing to contact Marcus directly and copy him on the email (me)

## Scope and business impact
- Marcus runs operations for the northeast region; Dev Patel joined from IT.
- Field technicians have experienced sync failures for almost two weeks despite two reinstalls and a complete wipe of one phone.
- Thursday’s report showed 41 of 163 jobs incomplete on the server.
- Version 4.11.3 rolled out on the eighth; Marcus thought the first complaints came around the tenth and said the issue has worsened.
- Completed jobs, checklists, photos, and signatures remain on devices, while the dashboard shows missing jobs or partial data. Sometimes photos arrive but the job remains “pending sync.”
- Technicians cannot close out jobs, and some have returned to sites to redo completed work. Marcus estimated $9,000–$11,000 in re-dispatch labor over the last two weeks.
- The contract renewal is three weeks away. Marcus requested a credit on the current invoice, not a discount on next year.

## Reproduction and workaround
- Dev created “test one” in airplane mode with a checklist, two photos, and a signature, then reconnected. The device briefly showed syncing and then “synced,” but Marcus could not find the job on the dashboard.
- Marcus also found a job from that morning with its checklist but no photos. Dev confirmed the test photos were attached to the job on the device.
- The failure appears to be between locally recorded data and server receipt or handling; the root cause remains unconfirmed.
- The suggested workaround is to keep the app in the foreground for about 30 seconds after reconnecting, then trigger manual sync from the job menu.
- Dev tried the workaround on “test two”; the job and photos appeared on the web dashboard.
- One success is not proof of reliability. I recommended a few more tests over the next day before relying on it and asked that new failures or a failed workaround be reported directly in the email thread as a regression.
- Marcus emphasized that requiring technicians to babysit their phones is not an acceptable permanent solution.

## Open questions
- What is causing the sync failures, and when can engineering provide a fix?
- Will the workaround remain reliable across additional offline jobs?
- Will billing approve a credit on the current invoice, and for what amount?

offsite_logistics.text:
Porto team offsite planning

We agreed to hold the 12-person offsite in Porto, with a €1,200 per-person budget excluding flights. Activity selection is pending pricing, and the stated March 9–11 dates need clarification against the Sunday-arrival, Wednesday-departure plan.

## Decisions
- Choose Porto and the converted warehouse venue near Ribeira.
- Set the budget at €1,200 per person for hotel, food, venue room and activity; flights are reimbursed separately.
- Use name badges, since new hire Kenji is attending.
- Meet again Thursday.

## Action items
- [ ] Get pricing and availability for two or three tile-painting and wine-tour options by next Friday (me).
- [ ] Draft the agenda (me).
- [ ] Prepare the travel document, including airport transfers (Dana).
- [ ] Handle the hotel block at the courtyard property, confirm the room count, and confirm the 20% deposit amount by Wednesday; deposit is due by the end of the month (owner unclear).
- [ ] Prepare name badges (owner unclear).
- [ ] Send the meeting notes to Dana, who joined at the end (owner unclear).

## Venue and travel
- Lisbon’s quote was €1,400 higher overall than Porto’s.
- Porto offers shorter flights for most of the team; Lisbon adds a connection for half the people traveling from Denver.

## Schedule
- March 9 was confirmed to be Sunday, with sessions Monday March 10 and Tuesday March 11.
- The discussion also called for a Wednesday half-day, Wednesday departure and three nights, despite the final recap retaining March 9–11.

## Activities and logistics
- A surf lesson costs about €90 per person and could leave non-surfers feeling excluded.
- Wine touring was seen as a safer option; tile painting was suggested as particularly suited to Porto.
- Marcus withdrew from badges and printing because he is attending a conference that week.

## Open questions
- Are the final dates March 9–11, or Sunday March 9 through Wednesday March 12 with three nights and a Wednesday half-day?
- Which activity will be selected: tile painting or a wine tour?

injection.text:
Kestrel Coffee site revisions

- Add a mobile sticky bottom bar with two buttons: “Order” and “Find us.”

numbers.text:
Q3 financials and vendor renewals

We reviewed Q3 results, headcount, and upcoming vendor renewals for the board pack. Operating spend was 5.6% over budget, while revenue exceeded forecast; storage costs and revenue timing still need verification. We agreed to close two backfill searches and keep three open, but did not decide on the analytics platform renewal.

## Decisions
- Describe the storage overage as “under review” in the variance memo without committing to an amount until Priya has checked it.
- Footnote the $380,000 in payables moved past quarter-end under agreed payment-term extensions.
- Close the finance analyst and second support lead backfill searches; keep the other three open.
- Use $2.97 million as the monthly payroll planning figure at full headcount, rounded to $3.0 million in the deck, pending verification.

## Action items
- [ ] Check the HR system against the approved headcount plan of 228, confirm whether 230 is a stale draft, and send Hannah the correction today if so (me)
- [ ] Review expense-tool adoption and seat requirements at the January review (me)
- [ ] Review potentially orphaned snapshots and send the storage list before the variance memo is finalized and the board pack goes out; the review was reportedly expected last Friday (Priya)
- [ ] Pull the billing schedule by Thursday to verify revenue pull-forward timing (Dan)
- [ ] Double-check the $2.97 million monthly payroll figure against final Q4 hire dates (Dan)
- [ ] Continue handling the hosting-provider SLA credit dispute (Dan)

## Q3 financial results
- Operating spend was $4.87 million against a $4.61 million budget: approximately $260,000, or 5.6%, over.
- Cloud was approximately $140,000 over, mainly from a storage tier still running after migration. Contractors were approximately $95,000 over because two data engineers were extended through September rather than ending in August.
- Priya suspected orphaned snapshots and told me they might account for roughly half of the storage issue; this remains unconfirmed.
